DETAILED ACTION
Notice of Pre-AIA  or AIA  Status
The present application, filed on or after March 16, 2013, is being examined under the first inventor to file provisions of the AIA .
Priority
Receipt is acknowledged of certified copies of papers required by 37 CFR 1.55.
Information Disclosure Statement
The information disclosure statement (IDS) submitted on 09/16/2020 is in compliance with the provisions of 37 CFR 1.97.  Accordingly, the information disclosure statement is being considered by the examiner.
Claim Objections
Claim 1 is objected to because of the following informalities: “configured to generating” should read “configured to generate” (line 1).  Appropriate correction is required.
Claim 2 is objected to because of the following informalities: “estimating a periodic noise waveform” should read “estimating the periodic noise waveform” (line 1).  Appropriate correction is required.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 101
35 U.S.C. 101 reads as follows:
Whoever invents or discovers any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof, may obtain a patent therefor, subject to the conditions and requirements of this title.
Claims 1-14 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 because the claimed invention is directed to an abstract idea without significantly more.
Claim 1 recites a method performed by an anesthetizing monitoring unit configured to generating an improved evoked electromyography response signal (ΣResponse), the method comprising: transmitting a stimuli signal (SStimuli) using an output port of the anesthetizing monitoring unit, receiving an evoked electromyography, EMG, response signal (SResponse), having a duration (TResponse), in response to the transmitted stimuli signal (SStimuli) using an input port of the anesthetizing monitoring unit, estimating a periodic noise waveform (SPeriodic), having the duration (TResponse), by using temporal segments of a noise signal (SNoise), generating the improved response signal (ΣResponse) by subtracting the noise waveform from the response signal (SResponse), which is using a computer as a tool to perform a mental process [MPEP 2106.04(a)(2)]. The limitation of generating an improved evoked electromyography response signal, as drafted, is a process that, under its broadest reasonable interpretation, covers performance of the limitation in mind but for the recitation of generic computer components. That is, other than reciting “performed by an anesthetizing monitoring unit”, nothing in the claim element precludes the step from practically being performed in the mind. For example, but for the “performed by an anesthetizing monitoring unit” language, “generating” in the context of this claim encompasses performing a method by computer that could be performed by the mind.
The limitation of transmitting a stimuli signal (SStimuli) using an output port of the anesthetizing monitoring unit is an insignificant extra-solution activity of using a computer as a tool to perform a mental process [MPEP 2106.04(a)(2)]. The limitation of transmitting a stimuli signal, as drafted, is a process that, under its broadest reasonable interpretation, covers performance as merely an insignificant extra-solution activity of a transmitting data from the abstract mental process of generating an improved evoked electromyography response signal, recited at a high level of generality and/or in a well-understood, routine, and conventional way.
The limitation receiving an evoked electromyography, EMG, response signal (SResponse), having a duration (TResponse), in response to the transmitted stimuli signal (SStimuli) using an input port of the anesthetizing monitoring unit is an insignificant extra-solution activity of using a computer as a tool to perform a mental process [MPEP 2106.04(a)(2)]. The limitation of receiving an evoked EMG response signal, as drafted, is a process that, under its broadest reasonable interpretation, covers performance as mere data gathering in order to generate an improved evoked electromyography response signal, recited at a high level of generality and/or in a well-understood, routine, and conventional way.
The limitation of estimating a periodic noise waveform (SPeriodic), having the duration (TResponse), by using temporal segments of a noise signal (SNoise), as drafted, is a process that, under its broadest reasonable interpretation, covers performance of the limitation in mind but for the recitation of generic computer components. That is, other than reciting “by an anesthetizing monitoring unit”, nothing in the claim element precludes the step from practically being performed in the mind. For example, but for the “by an anesthetizing monitoring unit” language, “estimating” in the context of this claim encompasses performing a method by computer that could be performed by the mind.
The limitation of generating the improved response signal (ΣResponse) by subtracting the noise waveform from the response signal (SResponse), as drafted, is a process that, under its broadest reasonable interpretation, covers performance of the limitation in mind but for the recitation of generic computer components. That is, other than reciting “by an anesthetizing monitoring unit”, nothing in the claim element precludes the step from practically being performed in the mind. For example, but for the “by an anesthetizing monitoring unit” language, “generating” in the context of this claim encompasses performing a method by computer that could be performed by the mind.

The limitation of splitting the noise signal (SNoise) into a number N of temporal segments (S1, S2, ... , SN), as drafted, is a process that, under its broadest reasonable interpretation, covers performance of the limitation in mind but for the recitation of generic computer components. That is, other than reciting “performed by an anesthetizing monitoring unit”, nothing in the claim element precludes the step from practically being performed in the mind. For example, but for the “performed by an anesthetizing monitoring unit” language, “splitting” in the context of this claim encompasses performing a method by computer that could be performed by the mind.

That is, other than reciting “performed by an anesthetizing monitoring unit”, nothing in the claim element precludes the step from practically being performed in the mind. For example, but for the “performed by an anesthetizing monitoring unit” language, “generating” in the context of this claim encompasses performing a method by computer that could be performed by the mind.

The limitation of the periodic noise template (STemplate) is generated by averaging discrete samples over the N temporal segments (S1, S2, … SN), as drafted, is a process that, under its broadest reasonable interpretation, covers performance of the limitation in mind but for the recitation of generic computer components. The limitation of displaying the anesthetized patient state to a user of the anesthetizing monitoring unit, as drafted, is a process that, under its broadest reasonable interpretation, covers performance as merely an insignificant extra-solution activity a generic display of feedback from the abstract mental process of generating an improved evoked electromyography response signal, recited at a high level of generality and/or in a well-understood, routine, and conventional way.

Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 102
The following is a quotation of the appropriate paragraphs of 35 U.S.C. 102 that form the basis for the rejections under this section made in this Office action:
A person shall be entitled to a patent unless –
(a)(1) the claimed invention was patented, described in a printed publication, or in public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
(a)(2) the claimed invention was described in a patent issued under section 151, or in an application for patent published or deemed published under section 122(b), in which the patent or application, as the case may be, names another inventor and was effectively filed before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
Claims 1-14 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) as being anticipated by US 20170245776 A1 (Kurtz et al.).
Regarding claim 1, Kurtz teaches a method performed by an anesthetizing monitoring unit (110) ([0022] “apparatus”) configured to generating an improved evoked electromyography response signal (ΣResponse) ([0002] “The present application relates to an apparatus, system and method for detecting evoked responses to a stimulus (a stimulus-response signal).”) the method comprising: transmitting a stimuli signal (SStimuli) ([0022] “plurality of stimuli”) using an output port ([0030] “output device”) of the anesthetizing monitoring unit, receiving an evoked electromyography, EMG, response signal (SResponse) ([0022] “receive the noisy signal to the plurality of stimuli”), having a duration (TResponse), in response to the transmitted stimuli signal (SStimuli) using an input port ([0022] “input device”) of the anesthetizing monitoring unit, estimating a periodic noise waveform (SPeriodic) ([0008] “the noise is quasi-stationary”), having the duration (TResponse) ([0006] “stimulating the patient with multiple stimuli, obtaining multiple time-based data series”), by using temporal segments of a noise signal (SNoise), generating the improved response signal (ΣResponse) by subtracting the noise waveform from the response signal (SResponse) ([0059] “The final waveform or averaged response (sometimes called the “final response”), is the estimate of the synchronized evoked response, with reduced noise. It will be understood that the type of evoked response will generally be dependent on the stimulus and on the subject. For example, if a subject cannot hear an auditory stimulus, then there would not be an evoked response to the auditory stimulus.”; [0056] “reduce the negatively correlated noise from the resultant average”).
Regarding claim 2, Kurtz teaches the method according to claim 1, wherein the step of estimating a periodic noise waveform further comprises: splitting the noise signal (SNoise) into a number N of temporal segments (S1, S2, ... , SN) ([0014] “divide the noisy signal into a plurality of responses to the plurality of stimuli”), generating a periodic noise template (STemplate) by aggregating the N temporal segments (S1, S2, ... , SN) ([0016] “estimate a statistic matrix for the plurality of responses”), wherein the periodic noise waveform (SPeriodic), is estimated by subsequently repeating the periodic noise template (STemplate) N times ([0017] “performing a multilevel discrete wavelet transform on individual responses in a loop for each scale of the multilevel discrete wavelet transform”).
Regarding claim 3, Kurtz teaches the method according to claim 2, wherein the periodic noise template (STemplate) is generated by averaging discrete samples over the N temporal segments (S1, S2, … SN) ([0059] “The final waveform or averaged response (sometimes called the “final response”), is the estimate of the synchronized evoked response, with reduced noise. It will be understood that the type of evoked response will generally be dependent on the stimulus and on the subject. For example, if a subject cannot hear an auditory stimulus, then there would not be an evoked response to the auditory stimulus.”).
Regarding claim 4, Kurtz teaches the method according to claim 1, wherein the method further comprises determining an anesthetized patient state by determining a neuromuscular function value using properties of the improved response signal (ΣResponse) ([0134-0135] “an MMN response depends on the consciousness state of the subject, in the awake pre-op state, we expect there to be a significant MMN, while in the anesthesia state, we do not expect there to be an MMN present”).
Regarding claim 5, Kurtz teaches the method according to claim 1, wherein the anesthetized patient state is a selection of any of insufficient anesthetic level, low anesthetic level, sufficient anesthetic level, normal breathing function, capable of sustaining breathing or in need of ventilator ([0135] “an MMN response depends on the consciousness state of the subject, in the awake pre-op state, we expect there to be a significant MMN, while in the anesthesia state, we do not expect there to be an MMN present.”).
Regarding claim 6, Kurtz teaches the method according to claim 4, wherein the properties of the improved response signal (ΣResponse) include amplitude value/s (AResponse’) ([0135] “peak amplitude”) and wherein the neuromuscular function value is determined by comparing a quota of amplitude value/s of the improved response signal (ΣResponse) and additional amplitude value/s to a set of predetermined amplitude value/s thresholds, wherein the additional amplitude values are selected from amplitude value/s of the stimuli signal (SStimuli) and historical amplitude value/s of the improved response signal (ΣResponse) ([0135] “An MMN response is determined to be present when the peak amplitude of the processed deviant response is statistically different than that of a standard response in the region of expected MMN response”).
Regarding claim 7, Kurtz teaches the method according to claim 1, further comprising displaying the anesthetized patient state to a user of the anesthetizing monitoring unit ([0062] “The output module 145 may output data in various formats as are known in the art, including, for example, output to a display 150 for review by a user of the system.”).
Regarding claim 8, Kurtz teaches the method according to claim 2, wherein the temporal segments (S1, S2, ... , SN) have a duration (TPeriodic) proportional to the noise signal (SNoise) ([0068] “by weighting data series or groups of data series in inverse proportion to their noise content”).
Regarding claim 9, Kurtz teaches the method according to claim 8, wherein the duration (TPeriodic) is selected using a strongest periodic noise component of the noise signal (SNoise) ([0009] “In this case, the group is greater than 8 seconds in duration. The drawback of this technique is that noise in evoked potential measurements is, in general, not stationary over an 8 second duration, especially when the time series is contaminated with interference from the patient's EMG caused by muscle activity.”; The time period with the most noise is selected, indicative of muscle activity.).
Regarding claim 10, Kurtz teaches an anesthetizing monitoring unit configured to generating an improved evoked electromyography response signal (ΣResponse), the anesthetizing monitoring unit comprising: an input port ([0022] “input device”), an output port ([0030] “output device”), and processing circuitry ([0140] “The machine-readable medium can contain various sets of instructions, code sequences, configuration information, or other data, which, when executed, cause a processor to perform steps in a method according to an embodiment of the disclosure.”) being configured to perform the method according to claim 1 (see rejection above).
Regarding claim 11, Kurtz teaches an anesthetizing monitoring system configured to determine an anesthetized patient state, the anesthetizing monitoring unit ([0022] “an apparatus for detection of an evoked response signal in noise”) comprising: an anesthetizing monitoring unit comprising an input port ([0022] “input device”) and an output port ([0030] “output device”), stimulating electrodes electrically coupled to the output port and being configured to receive a stimuli signal (SStimuli) from the output port and deliver the stimuli signal (SStimuli) to the anesthetized patient ([0058] “A sensor or sensors 115, for example an electrode or electrodes, are provided to the subject to detect a noisy signal including a response to the stimulus, which is sent to an input module 120”), receiving electrodes electrically coupled to the input port and being configured to obtain an evoked electromyography, EMG, response signal (SResponse) ([0059] “electrodes receive continuous data, sometimes referred to as “noisy data” or “noisy signal”. For each stimulus, a synchronized evoked response within the subject's brain will be generated.”), in response to the stimuli signal (SStimuli) ([0058] “response to the stimulus”) and a noise signal (SNoise) ([0059] “noisy signal”), from the anesthetized patient, the anesthetizing monitoring unit being configured to perform the method according to claim 1 ([0059] “this evoked response will also be detected by the electrodes but is generally hidden in the noisy signal. Embodiments of the system, apparatus and method herein are intended to separate the evoked response, or stimulus-synchronized component, (sometimes referred to as a “response”) from the non-synchronized components (i.e. noise).”).
Regarding claim 12, Kurtz teaches a computer program is provided comprising computer-executable instructions for causing an anesthetizing monitoring unit, when the computer-executable instructions are executed on a processing unit comprised in the anesthetizing monitoring unit, to perform the method according claim 1 ([0140] “The machine-readable medium can contain various sets of instructions, code sequences, configuration information, or other data, which, when executed, cause a processor to perform steps in a method according to an embodiment of the disclosure.”).
Regarding claim 13, Kurtz teaches a computer program product comprising a computer-readable storage medium, the computer-readable storage medium having the computer program according to claim 12 embodied therein ([0140] “Embodiments of the disclosure or portions thereof can be represented as a computer program product stored in a machine-readable medium (also referred to as a computer-readable medium, a processor-readable medium, or a computer usable medium having a computer-readable program code embodied therein).”).
Regarding claim 14, Kurtz teaches a carrier comprising the computer program according to claim 12, wherein the carrier is one of an electronic signal, optical signal, radio signal, or computer readable storage medium ([0140] “computer-readable medium”).
Conclusion
